A lot of that increase would come in the form of taxes. The law would force millions more people to pay taxes by raising the cost of purchasing health insurance; according to the Congressional Budget Office, it’d result in $3.3 trillion in additional federal spending per year.

And that’s not even factoring in the cost of operating the Obamacare exchange: The cost estimated by the Bureau of Budget Research so far has been $34.6 billion, nearly half of what’s expected to come from the exchange over the next 10 years under the proposed law. Putting all that into account, you end up with hundreds of trillions of dollars being spent on health care services annually over the next two decades. Worst of all, we don’t know what it actually costs buying health insurance, so that’s where this debate comes.

So what exactly goes wrong with the proposed law? Not exactly the most promising answer, honestly, but we'll segue. Remember, the whole idea is to allow people to buy insurance when they only have enough money to afford it. Originally proposed by the office of the Reagan administration in 1997, this concept isn't quite "real" at all — it's more a kind of private health insurance quasi-insurance fund, in the sense of " welfare." If you don't have enough money that you don't need to pay any extra taxes, you can just buy the plan without taxing on a certain percentage of the money that's been owed to you. Of course, if you ever find yourself running out of money, you can just turn the plan off and use it for whatever services you didn't originally owe it for. And if you have a serious medical condition or an event in the near future, you wouldn't be paying any extra taxes.

But then, in 2011, the House of Representatives responded, in part by taking advantage of the "free market" element of the Affordable Care Act, to propose a law that would allow people to buy insurance when they don't have lots of money to afford it. It turned out to be pretty successful, but it still has several problems. For one, the legislation seems like a another attempt by the federal government to impose a few more regulations on the market in order to see if it creates an incentive for those people who have money in their pockets to buy insurance. In other words, it works like this: The more regulations you impose, the more people will switch to plans like Medicaid and online health care exchanges, while fewer will stick to traditional models like free-for-all. As you might expect, once you've got more regulations, those people who enter the system get more incentives to do so.

And for another, the legislation seems like not a sound solution that could work in the long term. For example, a recent poll actually found that less than a third of Americans support a law allowing people to buy personal health insurance. Because personal insurance generally costs a lot more to purchase, compared to individual insurance, the poll found that only 4 in 10 Americans would support doing something like this.

The whole problem with passing this bill comes down to three factors: First, it's been delayed a few years; second, it hasn't yet passed; and third, it hasn't really gotten much of a media attention. There's been rumors that the bill might get through the Senate and even make it to the White House, but there hasn't been any real progress to make it a law. “FAA will continue to work closely with all of the clubs in question and stand ready to take any action that can be taken to ensure they stay true to the rules.”Marijuana has the potential to provide a major health benefit: A team of researchers have found that marijuana may potentially reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes, a diabetes-related cardiovascular condition in middle-aged adults. The researchers based their findings in a study of rats who received marijuana-containing blood sugar samples. Follow-up studies in weight-free-weight controls found no significant association between marijuana use and risk of heart disease, diabetes, and liver disease, and no effects occurred on weight gain.

The study was published in the Journal of Alcohol and Alcoholism Sciences. According to a statement from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, "The findings suggest that marijuana has the potential to reduce type 2 diabetes further than we have previously seen in large clinical studies."

Of course, for what it's worth, there's no safety or risk associated with marijuana, so you shouldn't try just yet.

But that's not all. It also could help treat certain types of disease: Research has suggested that marijuana can reduce the sedative effects of conventional drugs, such as morphine. In fact, it's worth noting that marijuana could be used as an antidepressamine to treat addiction problems as well as depression and anxiety.BOSTON (Reuters) - The world’s second largest private investment bank GIM on Tuesday suspended a chairman over allegations of swiping on wealthy investors, pulled out three of his colleagues and fired a top communications officer in exchange for more than $10 million in civil lawsuits.

The scandal, which sparked an angry reaction from investors, sent shares plunging.

“We are deeply disappointed by these allegations,” Michael Morlini, head of GIM’s private investment management group, said in a statement to Reuters. “There is a review of these allegations and we are committed to working with our clients to verify their authenticity.”

Morlini’s co-workers could not be reached for comment.

GIM, one of the world’s most prominent private investment banks, has seen its value more than double since 2008. In 2011, its gross market capital stood at $1.6 trillion, up almost 50 percent from the beginning of last year.

The scandal began in June, when several executives said they bribed wealthy and influential investor friends to offer rises of as much as 10 percent on GIM’s shares in exchange for completing a $38 million loan deal made with a U.K. hedge fund firm.

The Boston bank denied claims that the executives violated its ethics policy and said it was reviewing its policy to ensure that they did not have political motives.

“Our policy states that we do not believe anyone with any commercial interest should demand any change in our shares based on his or her personal beliefs,” Michael Moricelli, president and CEO of GIM’s global headquarters in Toronto, said in a statement.

“We have conducted a review of the matter and have concluded that the alleged actions were taken in violation of our ethical policy,” Moricelli added.

The bank, founded by $700 investors in 2001, has fallen more than 30 percent to $1.4 trillion so far this year.

Morlini, who was appointed as chairman after previous CEO Craig Williams resigned in June, said he was leaving the post on Wednesday due to a “proocial conflict” between his predecessor and the board group.

On Wall Street, GIM’s stock fell 14 percent, -48660736, to close at $69.75 a share.

“LOGGAL DAMAGES”

GIM faces more than $100 million in civil lawsuits over allegations that its executives snooked investors in exchange for a $137.2 million loan deal with Mercury Corporation to build a hotel in Santa Ana, Texas, near the border with the U.K.

Senator Jason Schier (D-Calif.), chairman of the Judiciary Committee, said GIM would have to pay legal damages to its investors.

“There are those who deserve to pay damages. We hurt them. There are others who deserve damages. It is time that this story comes to a close,” Scher said.

Friedman Capital, another major investor, said in a letter to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission that it would withdraw all of its bonds and investment insurance as a result of the scandal.

In 2010, researchers at Stanford University announced the development of the solar cell, the first device to generate electricity without requiring light, water, and a battery. The energy generated by solar cells is 95% clean and costs 70% less at a price of just $10.

Since the success of the solar cell, the industry has been in increasing demand for cheaper, low-carboncarbon energy sources, particularly reusable materials. Traditionalally-produced reusable materials—removable materials that can adapt to the changing environment—are highly expensive to create, can take several years to reproduce, and have a reputation for being harmful to the health and the environment. Recently, in response to the industry’s growing demands, a number of companies, ranging from universities to venture capital to military, are using 3D printing as a new technology for creating objects that weren’t built from scratch. This could help in robots, space, aviation, aviation, healthcare, medicine, and various other areas of the economy.

 3D printing made its debut in the mid-2000s. While 3D printed bones, skin, and mechanical parts have found numerous applications, particularly in robots, aviation, space, and so on, the potential of 3D printing seemed like a far away until a few months ago when researchers at the University of California, San Diego (USD) created the world’s first 3D-printed reusable brain.

At first glance, the brain’s shape looks similar like one made out of an organ. Instead of organs, the USD researchers have 3D printed a number of different materials to create its own reusable structure. The first step of 3D printing involves the chemical interspilling of two opposing thermoplastic materials, resulting in a ring-shaped structure.

(Yeah, here’s a list of the most interesting developments in 3D printing.)

The reusable brain is made out of a liquid thermoplastic (Arkopyolopentellite) and an A-linked thermoplastic (Llyydydodococotopentellite)—the two materials weighing between 80 and 100 nanometers. The two openings at the base of the structure, inserted directly into the thermoplastic, form a ring. The design also gives the brain a round shape so that it can support multiple brain nerves without interfering with each other, resulting in increased stiffness. The team has also improved the brain’s heat resistance.

Science reported on the discovery, which was published in the journal Applied and Material Physics.

“This research is very important to us and sets the foundation for others to design and implement reusable materials to solve similar problems,” said Brian Stoman, an assistant research professor at the USD non-profit Institute for Materials, Processes, and Engineering (IAP), based at the University of California, San Diego City. “We used a new process for producing thermoplastics to create the brain, and this lays the foundation for many similar work to come.”

Four bombs linked to a group of far-right Islamic Islamists set fire in the capital Accra during a day of protests for the resignation of Niger President Mohammed Gorpahehe.

The bombers killed 13 people and injured dozens, while tens of thousands of people were also injured, authorities said on Friday as protesters tried to defend their positions in the nearby city of Moroviee.

Police said the suspects, recruited from oil-richy neighbor Saudi Arabia, were arrested on a multiple charges and that the group had no intention to carry out the attacks.

“This was a terrible attack ... an intentional attack on the nation’s flag by two terrorists who had gathered masses to oppose the regime,” Interior Minister Inibou Jouda said in a statement.

Gorpaheee’s army has ruled the South East African nation of some 1.2 million people, and he took power there in March 2012 after a rapid rise in opposition, kicked off by allegations of widespread corruption and an inadequate human rights.

Nerve’s population is mainly Catholic and Orthodox Christians, though the minorities and some Sunnis adhere to a more moderate form of Islam.

BRADFUL MotivATION

Police said the bombers were members of a group of armed, gun-wield militants known as the Green Red Group, recruited from oil-richy Saudi Arabia.

It is the branch of two militant groups headed by Saudi Arabian billionaire Abdullah bin Hasham and Mohammed bin Muhammad Abali.

In the United States, Abali’s older brother, former Libyan President Moafad Abali, is in prison in New York City awaiting trial on terrorism and conspiracy charges.

“These heinous attacks represent a brutal attack on the foundations of our democracy,” Vice President Joe Biden said in a statement.

“The suspects who carried out the attacks were brought to justice and we will continue working to get Niger back on its important path toward full democracy,” Assistant Secretary for U.S. Africa Michael Cunnman said.

The suspects have been identified as Amad Abdullah, 22, Mohammed Ahmad, 30, and Baed Abdul Salah, 36. They have been arrested on charges of money laundering, threat to national security and ties to terrorist organizations, according to AFP news agency.

Police said 273 people had been arrested, including seven journalists, two government officials, one photographer, and several amounts of money were seized.

A spokeswoman for a security agency said it was too early to provide details on the exact motive for the attacks.

Dzens of anti-government protesters demanding the resignation of Niger Prime Minister Mohammed Gorpaheee march on a street outside the national parliament in Moroviee, Niger September 11, 2015. REUTERS/Mario Bouo/Files

The protests were the most intense demonstrations for a political change since Gorpaheee’s step down in March 2012 after a decade of devastating war.

Nerve is South East Africa’s most popular democratic republic, with 75 percent supporting change, according to a Reuters poll conducted just a few weeks before the country goes to vote on Wednesday.

But after a day of prayer, protesters took to the streets to set fires on buildings, destroyed shops and enter violent clashes with police. Some escaped the violence with rocks or detonated bombs.

In Accra, Ahmed Ali, a student, said he was beaten by police officers and thrown to the ground twice. “The police are against us. We are a freedom movement,” he said.

Many world leaders have endorsed the call for the end of Niger’s four-decade-old dictatorship.

But critics accuse the government of keeping silence on the opposition, which cites the killing of journalists, military detention and other human rights abuses that have sparked protests in other African countries.

Government forces and their allies have been using tar gas walls in key traffic areas such as the dusty river-bound capital Accra to separate protesters from the public.

Two police officers were killed on Tuesday as they clashed with opposition fighters, leading to an unprecedented spike of violence in the country since the end of the 1980s.

Gorpaheee has enjoyed a conflicted reputation, having publicly apologizedized for corruption and collating with his opponents during an election campaign.

But his rule has fostered a three-year spiral of war and terrorism that has left at least 300,000 dead and almost 500,000 people displaced, according to a World Health Organization estimate.

In Washington, new U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry took to Twitter to say, “We remain committed to fighting for the overthrow of the Niger regime.”

FIRERES, BOMBSS

As many as 10,000 protesters gathered outside parliament in a show of free speech in Accra. Some protesters set fires on government buildings, police said.

U.S. Vice President Mike Pence speaks ahead of the GSC-20 Group summit in Beijing, China October 17, 2012. REUTERS/Wang Yiu/File

Pence was speaking at a White House press conference ahead of the G-200 summit, designed to address global economic and security challenges, which will take place in October.

“The United States needs to increase our pressure on Iran to back down from its nuclear activities in a non-interventionive manner and to try to work out a peace solution for the Middle East that is fair and in line with the United Nations ban on developing nuclear weapons,” Pence told reporters.

The Obama administration has repeatedly urged Iran to slow down on developing nuclear weapons.

U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry on Sunday said the U.S. would meet with Iran in Belgium to press for it to slow down on developing nuclear weapons.

Meanwhile, Israeli Foreign Affairs Minister Benjamin Haronen on Tuesday said Israel was starting talks with Hamas on proposals for a two-state Palestinian solution that would strengthen peace efforts in the Middle East and the West Bank.

His comments were translated into Hebrew and quoted by the Israeli parliament.

“We believe that these are important steps toward solving the Middle East in peace and without armed conflict,” Haronen said.

The United States and Israel have sanctioned Iran and accuse the latter of seeking to undermine democracy in the region, which includes states led by Christians and Islamic minorities.

Fascs Hamas, Iran, and Israel have been involved in armed conflict in the Middle East since the 1970s.What do you call a black hole?

A black hole is the most powerful object in physics.

Over 30 million black holes are observed - about 400 million million times more powerful than the entire solar system.

The traditional perception of a black hole is to compare it to a giant star, a comet or meteor.

Actually, a black hole is as large as a lake and is virtually impenetrable, consisting mainly of a round cloud of heavy matter.

The main features of a black hole are motion of matter, gravity and magnetic resistance.

So, how did a black hole form?

Well, the hardest thing to say is how it came from.

Physists link the black hole to a chemical event called Enionization.

The theory behind Enunciation is that when two black holes are adjacent, some matter is broken apart and combined to form a black hole.

KABUL/MAQURAR (Reuters) - Afghan militants on Tuesday fired a suicide bombing on a major museum of Islam and a shelter for supporters of a minority religion, killing at least two security officers, the interior minister said but denied the cause of the attack.

Interior Minister Shahid Faad Abdullah told state television on Tuesday that militants threw a suicide bomb explosive on the Islamic Research Centre in Maqur province, six kilometres (10 miles) south of Kabul.

The ancient museum is a shelter for supporters of the Shiite form of the Islam, which stems from Afghanistan's religious conflict with Sunnis, a minority controlled by the Afghan Muslim Brotherhood, a militant group.

Abad said officials of the ARIC (Afghanistan's Museum of Islam) and a mosque in northern Kabul may also have been targeted in the bombing.

"There is no indication that there has been a threat to the museum, although the area is currently under a state of emergency, and all access to the museum has been closed by police," he said.

At least two security officers were killed in the bombing, a security source said. One security officer was hit with tank gunfire to the left hand, while the other was hit with electric gunfire to the hand's side, said the source on condition of anonymity.

It was too early for the cause of the attack to be identified, though an Afghan news agency said it was launched by the Afghan army.

In a paper in the UK's journal Science, Morgan et al. (2012) published a study of the brain function of patients suffering from repeated drug addiction. They used magnetic imaging technology to figure out which areas in the brain were affected by the effects of marijuana (more commonly known as cannabis). Their results revealed that marijuana- smokers were more likely to develop depression, anxiety, and food aversion symptoms compared to marijuana-smoking controls. More importantly, the researchers found that patients were not affected exclusively by the effects of marijuana on their brains. Instead, they focused on the nervfrontal and parietfrontal brain systems, which are thought to be over-activized by marijuana.

The study represents an important victory for researchers who have long explored marijuana as a potential treatment for alcohol addiction. This research also adds to the already growing body of evidence that is pointing toward medical marijuana as a potential therapeutic option for the treatment of anxiety disorders and alcohol addiction.

Since marijuana is legalized for recreational use, however, no clinical trials have been conducted with adult users. Since human trials are not very long-term, it has become clear that more studies are needed to determine the full list of risks, costs, and benefits of medical marijuana.A US District Court judge has ruled against the left-leaning Federal Telecommunications Commission, concluding that its "net neutrality" proposal is constitutional, and could pave the way for big tech companies like AT&T and Time Warner to adopt similar policies.

Judge Richard Colazo spoke out against elements of the FCC's net neutrality proposal, which he said was unfair and aimed at targeting politically offensive websites:

'Net neutrality' is a fundamental principle of modern life in the age of the Internet. It allows for open Internet traffic, equal access to information, and protects freedom of expression ... The FCC's proposal would undermine these principles, meaning that private users of the Internet will be required to turn off their exposure to the content that is politically offensive ... This measure is clearly aimed at enendering neo-Nazist groups like the Ku Klux Klan, the Nation for White Unity, or other such groups. In any case, the mere presence of the word net neutrality" at the title of the document is creative enough for the proponents to create the public image they hope to achieve.

Later, the Electronic Consumers Union of America (EUA) and the Electronic Media Freedom Project (EFR) released a statement, which quoted FCC executive director Jason Molman as explaining the court's ruling:

The proposal faces several problems. First, it is unconstitutional because it opens a free door for Internet providers to control the views of Web users. Second, it undermines the principles of net neutrality, which gives Internet providers the right to offer Internet services without violating the privacy of Web users. These principles are too old to change in light of the modern nature of the Internet, particularly in the age of increasingly political content. In addition, once politically offensive content is prevented from appearing on politically neutral websites, Internet providers can block the availability of political content.

Colazo's ruling is an important step forward on the path to a similar and much more direct attempt to control online content, the Freedraud Act, which requires social media services to block ad-feeded content that "has an intent to harm or degrade an individual." Oh well, but we're not likely to see this out of the way.In the past, we’ve invented stupid ways to store expensive music discs and computers in our pockets. But now, there’s an even smarter way to save money: at least one researcher has proven that he can make a tiny lens that sucks up heat from water in your body, allowing an eye to break without leaving you in pain.

Yūsuke Hayashi of the Tokyo Institute of Technology came up with a solution for helping breaking eyes. His concept, phyllopopil, consists of tiny strips of metal covered in a bottle of water. They're crafted with covalent molecules that stick to the strips like wires. The wires collect heat, which flows over to the surface of the eye, preventing it from breaking when the water is taken away. This seems like quite a cool idea, and it looks like you could actually save your eyes from a situation where the cooler water in your body isn’t enough to accommodate.

Hao’s research has been published in Nature Chemistry as "Heat-water-induced eyeglasses: the potential to improve optical performance through a cheaply manufactured material" (PDF file). He’ll have to complete a clinical trial in few years in order to make the device into a commercial product.

While the device looks cool and works, it’s not enough to replace a human eye. Hayashi plans to test it on a very small (one-inch) rat and see how it works in real conditions.

If you want to know more about Hayashi’s work, download the PDF and MP3 versions of the paper (via Sergle), or check out the video on the YouTube channel /Science Geek.

Republican leader tells Democrats to throw Trump over the back burner. Reports Politico: Majority Leader Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) said he has not reached universal consensus within the Republican leadership in the House on how to respond to President Trump's controversial remarks earlier this week. "I'm an American, and I've been an ally of him for years and I'm very friendly with him and I have spoken to him very, very politely," McConnell told Fox News' Chris Stewart. "But I think that, you know, the fact that the president's ranting in this way that he's ranting is fundamentally inconsistent with democracy, it's something that we're going to have as a party to look at. And for me, though, maybe he should take some time to put his head behind himself and say, 'You know, I don't have any right to say what I've said on Wednesday or what I've said on Friday,' and to actually sit here in this room and try to evaluate what I think are potential violations. I would have no complaint." McConnell's comments come just days after Republicans in the House of Representatives are trying to secure a loophole that allows them to short-block the president's repeal of the controversial Affordable Care Act -- a bill that has evaded a bipartisan vote since 1977. -- Jason Steinberg, The Washington Post

President Barack Obama is planning to hold a private meeting with Democrats in Congress next week in response to the recent shooting in Oklahoma, reports The Washington Post. In addition to a meeting with Vice President Mike Pence in his East Room and another in the Oval Room in New York, the White House plans to hold a meeting with congressional Democrats next week. The group will include at least six senior members of the administration, according to a source, a person close to the plans for the meeting told The Washington Post. The person familiar with the meeting told The Post on condition of remaining anonymous because of a potential conflict that could result in violation of a rule that requires officials not to talk to reporters. An administration official also will meet with House Speaker Paul Ryan (R-Wis.) to discuss the link between May's mass shooting in San Bernardino, Calif., and al-Qaida's growing presence. ... While Republican lawmakers are cooling off from the summer break to get ready for their fall break, they are likely to use the weekend as a respite for the fall session, during which the Senate is under pressure to find a consensus on critical issues as diverse as immigration reform, defense spending and our nation's budget. -- Melanie Bengilotti, The Washington Post

Colorado researchers say cannabis reduces Alzheimer. Reports CNN: As people become more aware of the dangers associated with drugs, researchers suggest that cannabis may be capable of reducing the risk of Alzheimer's disease in adults, including seniors.

Cannabinine—a hemp compound found in the brain that shows a range of neuromanipulatory effects in animals—has been long thought of as an anti-smoking drug, but few studies have shown the same rejuvenating effects of cannabis as other anti-addiction drugs (i.e., breaking the addiction cycle caused by repeated smoking). That said, new research suggests that the plant may actually be a valuable aid for seniors.

"There has been little evidence that a cannabis product has been shown to reduce Alzheimer risk in adults, but we are extremely excited about the results," says lead study author Aded Shawar, an assistant professor in the Department of Medical Medicine at the Fraser Institute of Neuromedicine at the State University of Colorado in Salt Lake City.

In the first study, Dr. Shawar and his colleagues included 15 healthy, middle-aged patients with Alzheimer's disease. The patients were allowed to sleep in a bath box, they were given 0.01 g of cannabis a day, and the brain was measured in an MRI scan. The researchers found that giving cannabis could reduce the levels of cingotin, a protein found in the brain that helps counteract the damage associated with pre-smoking exposure. They also found that the patients who received a cannabis-containing product were more likely to attend a treatment program for Alzheimer's disease. They were also found to have lower levels of hypatostin, a protein also involved in Alzheimer's disease, than those who were given mesetidine or claretine.

This finding raises the possibility that ingredients from the cannabis plant could be an interesting new option for both antidepressant and depression treatment in adult and senior people. Although this study was only a small trial, it's hoped that the results will eventually raise more awareness of the use of cannabis as assistance in mental health care. -- James W. In 2007, the Environmental Protection Protection Agency issued a guideline to reduce greenhouse gas (GH) emissions into the atmosphere from power plants; for example, in 2009, the Clean Energy Agency approved a guideline to reduce phosphorous emissions from water passing through power plants. In 2010, the American Power Provider Association issued a guideline requiring providers to use carbon-bearing materials.

But these efforts haven't always been good for electricity consumers. The rapid adoption of new technology is bound to increase competition, which could lead to even higher prices for electricity service. The authors write: "This presents challenges for the industry, which increasingly is shifting away from fossil fuels to alternative sources." Indeed, a recent study by the Electric Industry Association of America (ECIA) found that the rapid adoption of wind-powered plants has already hurt their competitors.

In addition, alternative energy has expanded at a record pace. According to a study by Columbia University's team, usage of renewable energy in the United States has nearly doubled between 1990 and 2010. As author Cameron McCullen explains:

"Renew energy use in the United States has expanded at record speed, with some of this due to the construction of energy-efficient office buildings and massive urban development; the increased ability to extract carbon pollution from fossil fuel sources and lower maintenance costs; and the abundance of new energy sources and alternative methods of energy production."

The growth has also dramatically raised energy prices. In articles posted on the American Renewable Society's blog, " Renewable Energy and the Food Short," Michael Herbert and Brian Hager explain its effects on the average household:

"The cost of natural gas for electricity has increased by 50 percent in some areas over the past 15 years. The price of crude oil has increased by almost half between 1990 and 2000, and rising prices of diesel fuel have put much-needed pressure on lower-income families. The average use of diesel fuel by motor vehicles has increased 40 percent in the past few years between the low and middle-income income groups."

Other energy sources -- such as fine wind, solar, fracking, and long-term storage -- are also more expensive and require government support.

Fortunately, the federal government is backinging the renewable energy movement. In 2008, President Obama ordered the release of $40 million to support renewable energy. The money goes to states that depend on a significant portion of the electricity they receive to come from these energy sources. In states that generate more than 80 percent of their electricity from fossil fuels, natural gas and moderate wind power are the only sources of less than 1.5 percent of their electricity.

But a federal grant on the scale of this report could go a long way toward making renewable energy a mainstream industry. Until it does, we'll have to continue to see it as a tool for combating global climate change and solving food shortages by reducing carbon pollution and greenhouse gas emissions into food systems.

National Journal of Medical Research, online: https://doi.org/10.1036/s114054.2015.000004A new mixed nanoparticle made of gold and aluminum is resistant and able to survive fire even at low temperatures, according to a study published in the journal Nature Physics.

The finding could have significant implications for solar and wind-based energy storage as well as some industrial applications, including systems relying on renewable energy.

"Our results show that the material can survive fire even at temperatures exceeding 100 C, 60, or 300 C. This should help increase its potential for use as a fire absorber in such applications as medical labs, aircraft, and processes for cleaning debris caused by fire," the authors write.

Goldatin netotites, which are made from elements of the gold tree, can be resistant, stronger, and less expensive than other thermoplastic materials. By mixing the material with phyllhydydydthyl aldehyde — a chemical that plays important roles in chemical reactions — the resulting nanoparticle gains more thermal properties and becomes more resistant.

To modify the nanoparticle structure to its shape, the researchers added a layer of foam containing chitosan to the material that acts as a fire-spening layer. The presence of this layer could make the material more fire-resistant at lower temperatures.

The researchers exposed the material to highly intense light in fluorescent chambers before measuring in a microelectrode. They observed that the fire-resistant properties of the modified nanoparticle were up to 60 percent greater than a control material that was exposed to 30 times more intense light.

"The present results demonstrate how similar techniques in this field can be applied, and also suggest that this new material could be used as a useful form of insulation for solar and wind-based energy storage, for example, in nuclear systems," the authors write.

The research was conducted by international teams including scientists from the University of Michigan, the University of Michigan, the University of Oxford, Oxford University (UK), Zhejiang University (China), University of North Carolina (USA), and the University of Barcelona (Spain).

The research was funded by the Department of Energy, Industry and Technology (DEIF). Although giving away tax credits is an obvious way to make the life better for lower-income Americans, a Republican president would move forward with legislation to expand tax credits for those earning between $50,000 and $100,000. The Republican president would also move forward to repeal the consumption tax, a tax break that would disproportionately affect low-income families.

Fight campaign finance

Big money and campaign contributions are by far the most powerful forces in Washington. They play an inordinateate influence in elections. A recent report by the U.S. Government Accountability Office found that interest groups deliberately interfered in the election process in order to gain tens of millions of dollars.

Republican and Democratic candidates have set different priorities on the transparentization of election processes and fighting fraud at the federal level. If in office, a Republican president would take multiple steps to fight fraud at the federal level, including the Federal Election Commission and the Department of Justice‘s campaign finance unit.

Credit card reform

Depending on how much money you have in credit card accounts, and how much you want to borrow, the overall cost of your credit card can be higher for some people than they’d prefer. But decades of outdated pay-at-no-interest rules mean that people often lose their loans when they borrow too much.

Making matters worse, credit card systems are not only vulnerable, but corrupt. A study by the American Civil Liberties Union found that more than 50 percent of card transactions that totaled over $1.5 million were found to have been fraudulent (Hillary Clinton even said during the campaign that the credit card systems were “pork boxes”).

A future Republican president would launch an all-throated crackdown against credit card fraud, including a law to require banks to be transparent.

Reform the tax code

If income tax reform is the priority of both Republican and Democratic candidates, it’s no surprise that Americans at the poorest end of society have been named as a target for tax reform in recent years. But a recent report from the Congressional Budget Office paints a grim picture of how rich Americans pay higher tax bills at the cost of much less income.

According to CPO, the median tax rate for Republicans increased from $16,582 in 2009 to $7,474 in 2013. Catch in contrast: the median tax rate for Democrats jumped from $14,762 in 2011 to $9,229. If you were to be a three-person family making $400,000 a year, the median tax rate for Democrats would increase more than twice that much.

Rich families are being unfairly affected by the same kinds of government policies that crippled the economy through the financial crisis and Great Recession in the 1990s. A Republican president would propose lowering the median personal tax rate to 12.5 percent.

A Republican president would take steps to improve public health and social security

The implementation of the Affordable Care Act and the repeal of Obamacare made progress, but public health care remains in progress, with access to coverage a problem for millions of Americans who are in particular poverty. A 2013 study conducted by the NAACP found that 70 percent of college students do not receive medication until after they graduate, that 2.4 million high school students do not have a diabetes clinic in their school district, and that 1 in five girls are denied contraceptive tests in the first 3 years of school. Young Americans pay up to $3,000 a year in student loans because of lack of access to medical care. A MIT report released in February 2014 predicted that “3,000 more low-income families will not have access to public health care” as a result of the implementation of Obamacare.

A Republican president would take steps to address these problems, including spending as much as $1.1 trillion on public health care, which was originally promised by President Obama, but has not yet been implemented.

Create or otherwise provide new tax exemptions for billionaireaires

According to the Treasury Department, the U.S. wealthiest citizens now account for $1.7 trillion, 20 percent of the global GDP. Their greatest tax exemptions are often found in tax-exempted corporations and hedge fund funds.

Congress has proposed a number of laws mandating corporations to pay up to 70 percent of the taxes they collect. To date, these proposals have gone nowhere. A Republican president would introduce a bill that would require all companies to pay taxes of at least 70 percent.

Lowere taxes on the rich

In order to address the inequality of wealth among ordinary Americans, a Republican president would have to lower taxes on the rich. According to the Council on Budget, more than half of the 100 wealthiest people on the planet have net worth of $2.6 trillion a year.

There is an area in the brain, known as a white cortex in the neuroscience, that helps us balance attention and distraction. This area also provides essential energy for muscle function. Now, researchers have figured out how height, weight, and sex can affect this key component of intelligence.

People who have larger brain centers are more effective on cognitive development tests and better in other cognitive tests, the researchers found in a study published online this month in the American Journal of Computing and Psychology. (Why Small Brain Centers May Hurt Your Intelligence)

The study is the first study of its kind ever to explore how brain centers respond to size.

In the past, what researchers have been saying is that people of any size group are going to be undercognized,” said Millie Weilie, a computer scientist at the University of North Carolina in Long Beach. “If you’re a 6-foot-3 man, 4-foot-2 woman, 5-foot-1 woman, etc., or whatever it is, you’re going to be undercognized. This new study breaks apart this very common assumption that a larger white center harms cognitive ability, too.”

To break down those common assumptions, the researchers asked more than 30 people from various groups of age — 25, 40, and older to complete a task of choice in a week. They were asked to write down potential answers and report their attempts to solve them.

“[What we wanted to see was] how good you were at this task, how often were you getting the right answer,” said Weile, the study’s co-author and author. The research was funded by the Heidler Project for Social Science. “So we asked them, ‘Okay, we have a task, and how good have you been at coming up with the answer?’”

Then, after the researchers had completed their task, they asked each of the participants to perform a 15-minute alternate task, designed to find out some of what cognitive problems they might be experiencing. They used brain MRI to measure the brain activity of each of the 30 people selected for the study to do so.

The researchers found differences in the activity that occurred between two different groups of size. For example, participants who had the more short brains of the two groups (on average, 1.6 feet 4 feet 2 inches) had neural activity significantly lower than those who had the longer brains.

Interestingly, however, there was no significant difference in the performance of the alternative task, which involved multiple participants trying to find different answers to the same problem.

The findings are yet latest in a long line of research suggesting that larger brain centers can make people better on widely used cognitive tests.

In the late 1990s, a team at the University of North Carolina in Charlotte reported that people who have larger brain centers tended to better performance on the IQ test, a test of language ability. A few years later, a group of graduate students at Stanford University reported that students with larger brain centers tended to better performance on the speech ability test, a common test of verbal ability.

And in 2010, a group of 75 students and 100 nongraduate students at the University of Iowa, in Cedar Moines, Iowa, also found that those who had larger brain centers tended to a better performance in a test of word memory and visual memory.

“This is somewhat surprising, but certainly encouraging,” Jeffrey Miller, a graduate student from the Iowa study’s team, wrote in a paper published in the Journal of Social Science. “I was initially surprised by the results, but I think it’s important that we find out more about how the effects of differences in brain size might work differently between men and between women.”

Regardless of its results, the study should give people a doorolt to do more to improve their cognitive abilities, including losing some weight, getting involved in regular fitness classes, doing a lot of exercise, and eating a 12-calorie diet.

One benefit of pumping up brain size is probably increased concentration, said Daniel Zcherhick, an assistant professor of social science at the University of Virginia, and a fellow at the Gordon Gordon Institute, whose lab wasn’t involved with the research.

“The theory is that people have larger brain centers,” he said. “They become more relaxed and career. When they’re under certain types of stress, whether it’s a decrease in body fat, stress, distraction in the form of email, etc., it’s better to sit down back and relax and think about whatever that stress might be.”

The researchers plan to repeat the study with more years of data. A next study will also test for a variety of factors that could be affecting the brain’s white center activity, such as body fat, overall age, the sexual orientation of the participants, and the amount time the participants spend in school and work.
